recent_posts.title: Small Safety Improvements in the C++ 26 Core Language – MC++ BLOG
recent_posts.summary: C++26 introduces three key safety improvements to address common programming pitfalls: preventing binding returned references to temporaries, converting uninitialized reads from undefined behavior to erroneous behavior with automatic initialization, and making deletion of pointers to incomplete types ill-formed unless they have trivial destructors. These changes help catch dangerous patterns at compile time and provide safer defaults for memory management.

recent_posts.title: Contracts: Evaluation Semantic – MC++ BLOG
recent_posts.summary: Explores the four evaluation semantics for C++ contracts: ignore, observe, enforce, and quick-enforce. Covers the differences between checking and terminating semantics, explains contract violation handlers and their customization options, and details the std::contracts::contract_violation interface that provides information about contract violations including location, kind, and evaluation context.

recent_posts.title: Contracs: A Deep Dive – MC++ BLOG
recent_posts.summary: Contracts in C++26 provide a formal way to specify and verify software component interfaces through preconditions, postconditions, and invariants. The feature includes four evaluation semantics (ignore, observe, enforce, quick-enforce) that can be configured at compile time, link time, or runtime. Contract violations occur when predicates return false, throw exceptions, or fail to be constant expressions at compile time. Current restrictions apply to virtual functions, defaulted/deleted functions, and constructors/destructors, with preconditions evaluated after parameter initialization and postconditions evaluated before local variable destruction.

recent_posts.title: n): Bureaucracy – The German Disease – MC++ BLOG
recent_posts.summary: A personal account of navigating Germany's healthcare bureaucracy while dealing with ALS, highlighting systemic inefficiencies that create barriers for patients seeking medical equipment and care. The author describes how bureaucratic delays often render assistive devices useless by the time they're approved, and argues that the system favors those with resources and persistence, leaving vulnerable populations underserved.

recent_posts.title: Data-Parallel Types: Algorithms – MC++ BLOG
recent_posts.summary: C++26's data-parallel types library introduces four specialized algorithms for SIMD vectors: min, max, minmax, and clamp. The min and max functions perform element-wise comparisons between two SIMD vectors, while minmax returns both minimum and maximum results as a pair. The clamp algorithm constrains each vector element within specified bounds. These algorithms enable efficient vectorized operations for performance-critical applications, though some implementations may have compiler compatibility issues.

recent_posts.title: n): An Emergency Call – MC++ BLOG
recent_posts.summary: A personal account of an ALS patient's emergency hospitalization due to pneumonia complications. The author describes experiencing severe breathing difficulties when mucus blocked their lungs, requiring emergency medical intervention and hospitalization. After treatment with antibiotics and inhalation therapy, they made a full recovery. The post emphasizes the unpredictable and dangerous nature of ALS complications, particularly respiratory issues that can develop suddenly.

recent_posts.title: Data-Parallel Types: simd_mask – MC++ BLOG
recent_posts.summary: The simd_mask type enables conditional execution of operations on SIMD vectors in C++. It works with the where expression to selectively apply operations to vector elements based on boolean conditions. The mask contains truth values corresponding to each SIMD vector element, allowing for efficient conditional processing. Examples demonstrate creating masks from predicates and using them to conditionally modify vector elements, such as computing absolute values by negating only negative elements.
